items.title: Lesson 2 Focus Question: How is electrical energy used and paid for in a home?

answer.html: It is transformed into other useful forms: light (lamps), thermal energy (heaters, kettles, dryers), motion (motors), and stored chemical energy (battery charging). A household pays for it by the kilowatt-hour: 𝐸= 𝑃𝑡, with 𝑃 in kW and 𝑡 in hours.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It? (a): How are electric circuits being used to transform energy in a night photograph of a football stadium?

answer.html: The floodlights are electric lamps: circuits transform electrical energy into radiant (light) energy plus thermal energy. The scoreboard and sound system also transform electrical energy into light and into sound (kinetic energy of air).

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 14: Explain why the heating coil of an electric kettle gets hot when it is switched on

answer.html: Current flows through the resistive coil. The moving electrons collide with the atoms of the coil and make them vibrate faster, so electrical energy becomes thermal energy (𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅) and the coil's temperature rises.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It? (b): What potential difference is needed to keep a current going around a loop of superconducting wire?

answer.html: Zero. A superconductor has zero resistance, so 𝛥𝑉= 𝐼𝑅= 𝐼(0) = 0 and the current continues without a source.

items.title: Lesson 2, Cause and Effect: Poster proposing superconducting cables for a city's subway power supply (open-ended)

question.html: This asks for a student-made product, so the solution here is the content a good poster would contain (a sample). Cause: Replace the copper supply cables with superconducting cables, so 𝑅≈0. Effects: The 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 heating loss in the cables falls to nearly zero, so almost all the energy generated reaches the trains. That means lower electricity bills, less fuel burned and less pollution per kWh delivered. Thinner cables could carry the same current. Trade-offs: Present superconductors must be kept far below room temperature (liquid-nitrogen temperature or colder), so cooling equipment costs energy and money, and installation is expensive.

answer.html: A poster should say that superconducting cables would remove 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 losses (an efficiency, cost and environmental gain), and should also mention the cooling cost and equipment needed.

items.title: Lesson 2, Check Your Progress Problem 35: A wind turbine drives a generator that charges a battery, which powers a street lamp at night. Name the forms of energy

answer.html: (1) Wind to generator: kinetic energy of the air becomes kinetic energy of the rotor, then electrical energy. (2) Generator to battery: electrical energy is stored as chemical energy. (3) Battery to lamp: chemical energy becomes electrical energy, then radiant (light) energy plus thermal energy.

body.html: At fixed voltage, 𝑃= (𝛥𝑉)<sup>2</sup> / 𝑅, so less power means more resistance.

answer.html: The "low" setting, because it uses less power at the same 120 V, which requires a larger resistance (less current).

items.title: 37: Evaluate the impact of research to develop more efficient LED lighting

answer.html: More efficient lamps turn a larger fraction of electrical energy into light, so less is wasted as thermal energy. Society gains lower electricity bills and a smaller demand on power plants; the environment gains because less fuel is burned (less pollution and carbon dioxide). Costs include the expense of replacing fixtures and the disposal of old lamps.

𝑃<sub>wire, 120</sub> = (30 A)<sup>2</sup>(0.10 𝛺) = 90 W,

answer.html: At 240 V the current is half (15 A instead of 30 A) and the wire heating is one quarter (22.5 W instead of 90 W), so wiring is safer and less energy is wasted.

items.title: Lesson 2 Focus Question: How do we use electrical energy?

answer.html: We transform it into other useful forms: light (lamps), thermal energy (heaters, stoves, hair dryers), motion (motors), and stored chemical energy (battery charging). Utilities deliver it over high- voltage lines and sell it by the kilowatt-hour.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It? (a): How are electric circuits being used to transform energy in the image of Earth at night?

answer.html: The lights visible from space are electric lamps (street lights, buildings, homes). Electric circuits there transform electrical energy into radiant (light) energy, plus some thermal energy.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 14: Explain why the appliances heat up when they are turned on

answer.html: Current flows through the appliance's resistive element. The moving electrons collide with the atoms of the element, making them vibrate faster, so electrical energy becomes thermal energy (𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅) and the temperature rises.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It? (b): State the resistance of a superconductor
Lesson 2, Cause and Effect: Brochure on superconducting power cables (open-ended)

question.html: This asks for a student-made product, so the solution here is the content a good brochure would contain. Cause: Replace ordinary cables with superconducting cables, so 𝑅≈0. Effects: The 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 loss in the line drops to nearly zero, so more of the generated energy reaches users (higher efficiency, less fuel burned, less pollution and carbon dioxide per kWh delivered, lower costs). Lines could carry much more current in thinner cables, and long-distance power transfer would be more practical. Trade-offs: Present superconductors must be kept very cold (below about 100 K), so cooling systems cost energy and money; materials and installation are expensive.

answer.html: A brochure should state that superconducting cables would remove 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 heating losses (a large efficiency, cost and environmental gain), and should also note the cooling cost and equipment needed.

items.title: Lesson 2, Check Your Progress Problem 35: Car engine drives a generator that charges the battery, which powers headlights. Forms of energy?

answer.html: (1) Engine to generator: chemical energy of fuel becomes thermal energy, then kinetic (mechanical) energy, then electrical energy. (2) Generator to battery: electrical energy is stored as chemical energy. (3) Battery to headlights: chemical energy becomes electrical energy, then radiant (light) energy plus thermal energy.

body.html: At fixed voltage, 𝑃= (𝛥𝑉)<sup>2</sup> / 𝑅, so more power means less resistance.

answer.html: The hot setting, because it uses more power at the same 120 V, which requires a smaller resistance (more current).

items.title: 37: Evaluate the impact of research to improve power transmission lines

answer.html: More efficient lines (lower resistance, such as superconductors, or better high-voltage design) waste less energy as 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 heat. Society gains lower electricity costs and more reliable supply; the environment gains because less fuel must be burned (less pollution and carbon dioxide) and fewer power plants are needed. Costs and impacts include expensive materials, cooling needs, and land use for new lines.

items.title: 38: Why do an electric range and a water heater use 240 V instead of 120 V?

body.html: For a given power 𝑃= 𝐼𝛥𝑉, doubling the voltage halves the current. These appliances need a lot of power (several kW).

answer.html: At 240 V the same power needs only half the current, so the wires carry less current and lose less energy as 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 heat (and can be thinner and safer, with smaller breakers), compared with 120 V.

items.title: 41: During a "brown-out" the voltage is reduced. What is being saved?

body.html: For fixed-resistance devices, 𝑃= (𝛥𝑉)<sup>2</sup> / 𝑅, so lowering the voltage lowers the power demanded. The line current also drops, so 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 losses drop.

answer.html: Power (the rate of energy use, and so fuel and generating capacity) is saved, because devices draw less power at lower voltage. The drawback is that lights dim and heaters or motors work less well.
